title: Process Control
lead: Stop processes safely with signals, target them by PID or name, and adjust CPU priority.
objectives: You explain that `kill` sends signals and distinguish SIGTERM from SIGKILL.
You verify a PID and command line before targeting a process.
You understand `pkill`, `nice`, `renice`, and their permission limits.

sections.title: Signals: kill, SIGTERM, and SIGKILL
body: `kill PID` sends **SIGTERM (15)** by default. It gives the process a chance to shut down cleanly and save data. If it does not respond, **SIGKILL (9)** is the last resort; a process cannot catch or ignore it.
`kill` sends a signal; it does not always mean “kill.” Verify the PID and command with `ps` or `pgrep` first. In particular, `kill -9` and targeting multiple processes can cause data loss.

commands.what: Sends SIGTERM to the specified PID.
commands.where: When closing an application or stopping it cleanly.
commands.why: It gives the process a chance to clean up and save data.

commands.what: Immediately terminates the process through the kernel.
commands.where: Only as a last resort when SIGTERM does not work.
commands.why: The process cannot catch it; unsaved work may be lost.

sections.tip: Name the signal explicitly: `kill -TERM PID`. Then check with `ps -p PID` to see whether the process exited.
sections.warn: Do not signal a process on a production server or under a process manager without verifying its PID. Never target PID 1 or an unknown system process.

sections.title: Find and target processes by name
body: `ps` gives you a process snapshot; `pgrep` searches for PIDs by name. `pkill` sends signals to matching processes. Check `pgrep -a` first because a name match may affect more processes than expected.
`pkill -TERM -x worker` targets only exact process-name matches. Use `-f` to match the full command line only when needed; it carries a higher risk of matching too broadly.

commands.what: Lists the PID and command for processes named exactly worker.
commands.where: Before sending a signal to verify the target.
commands.why: It reduces the chance of targeting the wrong PID or a similarly named process.

commands.what: Sends SIGTERM to processes named exactly worker.
commands.where: When stopping a verified group of processes.
commands.why: It requests a graceful shutdown without entering each PID.

sections.tip: Run the same match with `pgrep -a` before using `pkill` so you can review every target.
sections.danger: `pkill -f` matches any part of a command line. Do not use it with a short or generic pattern.

sections.title: CPU priority: nice and renice
body: The nice range is **-20 to 19**: a higher value means a lower CPU priority. Regular users can lower the priority of their own processes; raising it usually requires administrator privileges.
`nice` starts a new command with a chosen value; `renice` changes the value of a running process. This affects CPU scheduling, but does not limit memory or CPU usage.

commands.what: Starts a new command with nice value 10.
commands.where: For background work such as backups.
commands.why: It lets interactive work get CPU time more easily.

commands.what: Sets a running process's nice value to 10.
commands.where: When lowering the priority of a running background task.
commands.why: It changes CPU priority without restarting the process.

sections.tip: Nice value and process state are different; inspect them separately with `ps -o pid,ni,stat,comm -p PID`.

t01.text: Use `grep` to find user alice's processes in `~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`.
t01.hint: The file starts with a `USER` column; try `grep alice ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`.

t02.text: Find the PID of the `python3` process in the snapshot.
t02.hint: In the line from `grep python3 ~/lab/ps_snapshot.txt`, the second field is the PID.

t03.text: Predict how many lines contain `python3`, then verify with `grep -c`.

t04.text: Save a graceful shutdown plan in `~/lab/term_plan.txt`: use `kill -TERM` for PID 2210.

t05.text: Write an example in `~/lab/priority_plan.txt` that starts a backup with lower CPU priority.

t06.text: Add PID verification and a wait after SIGTERM; mention SIGKILL only as a last resort.

t07.text: For ticket #5301, write a short note that PID 2210 is `python3` and SIGTERM should be tried first.

vm.intro: Run these commands only in your own test VM. Do not signal an arbitrary PID; verify the process name and PID.

v01.title: Start a controlled process
v01.text: Start a short-lived test process, note its PID, and verify it with `ps`. Stop it when done.

blocks.expected: The PID and sleep command are visible.

differs: The shell may also print a job number; the PID is on the `echo $!` line.
The PID will differ; do not expect a fixed number.

v02.title: Try SIGTERM first
v02.text: Use the real PID of the test process you just started. Send SIGTERM, wait briefly, and verify that it exited.

blocks.cmd:
kill -TERM PID
sleep 1
ps -p PID || echo 'process stopped'

differs: Replace PID with the number from v01; do not run the literal word `PID`.
If the process remains, verify the PID; do not signal another process.

v03.title: Inspect the nice value
v03.text: Start a test process with lower priority, read its NI value in `ps`, and then stop your process.

blocks.expected: The NI column shows 10 and the command column shows sleep.

differs: Column headings may be aligned differently by `ps`; the NI value should be 10.
Stop only the PID started by your shell.

q1.q: Which signal does `kill PID` send by default?
q1.explain: SIGTERM is the default signal; it asks the process to shut down cleanly.

options: As a last resort when SIGTERM fails
q2.explain: SIGKILL cannot be caught and leaves no time for cleanup, so use it only as a last resort.

q3.q: What happens when the nice value rises from 0 to 10?
q3.explain: A higher nice value means lower priority in CPU scheduling.

q4.q: What should you do before targeting a process with `pkill`?
q4.explain: Reviewing the matches confirms the target and reveals possible side effects.

summary: `kill` sends SIGTERM by default; SIGKILL is a last resort.
Verify the PID and command with `ps` or `pgrep -a` before sending a signal.
`nice` sets priority at launch and `renice` changes it for a running process; higher nice means lower priority.

glossary.meaning: A control notification the kernel sends to a process.
The unique process identifier of a running process.
A value that affects a process's relative priority in CPU scheduling.
